title: Projection Bias
description: People assume others think, feel, and value the same things they do, projecting their own mental states onto others.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: People assume others think, feel, and value the same things they do, projecting their own mental states onto others.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A detail-oriented boss assumes everyone cares about tiny formatting errors as much as they do.
A person who would never lie assumes others are equally honest, making them vulnerable to manipulation.
You buy a gift that you would love, convinced the recipient will too, and are surprised when they’re indifferent.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Surprise when others make different choices with the same information.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I can’t understand why they did that.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You’re shocked when someone disagrees with a position you hold deeply.
You feel that your reasoning is universally self-evident.
You rarely ask others for their perspective; you assume you already know it.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Using one’s own mental state as a reference point is cognitively efficient. The false consensus effect (Ross, Greene, & House, 1977) shows we overestimate how many share our views. Epley et al. (2004) detail how anchoring on one’s own perspective shapes judgments of others.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Before attributing motives, explicitly ask: “What’s your take on this?”
Deliberately list three ways a reasonable person could see the opposite.
In negotiations, avoid assuming the other party’s priorities are the same as yours.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking you’re good at “reading people” and therefore don’t need to ask. Projection is more common than accurate intuition.
Over-correcting and assuming everyone is completely different from you, leading to stereotyping.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A product designer loves minimalist interfaces. She spends months crafting a sleek app, confident users will appreciate the clean design. Upon launch, users complain that essential features are hidden. She projected her own preference for minimalism onto a general audience who values discoverability.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The map you’re holding is your own. Before guiding others, ask to see theirs.
